parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a field does - it tells you what force would act if you placed a small test mass there, so focus on force for each 1 kg.
parts.proper_answer: Gravitational field strength is the gravitational force per unit mass acting on a small test mass.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What field strength means**
Think of the field as a way to describe how strong gravity is at a point in space. You imagine placing a tiny 1 kg test mass there and asking what force it would feel. So strength is defined per kilogram of test mass.

Step 2: **Exact definition**
That gives $$g = \frac{F}{m}$$ in words: force per unit mass. The unit is $\text{N kg}^{-1}$, which is the same as $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem: The nearest star to the Sun is Proxima Centauri. This star has a mass of $2.5 \times 10^{29} \text{ kg}$ and is a distance of $4.0 \times 10^{13} \text{ km}$ from the Sun. The Sun has a mass of $2.0 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: State why Proxima Centauri may be assumed to be a point mass when viewed from the Sun.

markscheme_points.text: radius/diameter/size (of Proxima Centauri) $\ll$ /is much less than $4.0 \times 10^{13} \text{km}$/separation (of Sun and star) or (because) it is a uniform sphere

hints: Hint 1: Compare the two length scales in this situation - the physical size of the star itself and the huge distance between the Sun and the star.
parts.proper_answer: The radius of Proxima Centauri is much less than the separation of $4.0 \times 10^{13} \text{ km}$, so it may be treated as a point mass.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **When a point mass is allowed**
You can treat an extended sphere as a point mass at its centre when its own size is tiny compared with the distance to where you measure the field. Then all the mass acts as if concentrated at the centre.

Step 2: **Apply to this star**
Here the separation is $4.0 \times 10^{13} \text{ km}$, enormously larger than the radius of any star. From the Sun, Proxima Centauri looks like a point, so the point-mass formula $g = GM/x^2$ is valid.

parts.text: the gravitational field strength due to Proxima Centauri at a distance of $4.0 \times 10^{13} \text{ km}$,
hints: Hint 1: Start by listing the mass creating the field and the separation, and check the distance units carefully against the SI units needed for $G$.
Hint 2: Recall how field strength links the mass of the source to the inverse square of distance from its centre: $g = GM/x^2$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Convert distance to metres**
$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11} \text{ N m}^2 \text{ kg}^{-2}$ needs metres. $$x = 4.0 \times 10^{13} \text{ km} = 4.0 \times 10^{13} \times 10^3 \text{ m} = 4.0 \times 10^{16} \text{ m}$$ Mass of source, Proxima Centauri, $M = 2.5 \times 10^{29} \text{ kg}$.

Step 2: **Field strength due to Proxima**
For a point mass: $$g = \frac{GM}{x^2}$$ $$g = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 2.5 \times 10^{29}}{(4.0 \times 10^{16})^2}$$ $$g = 1.0 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N kg}^{-1}$$ This is directed towards Proxima Centauri.

parts.text: the gravitational force of attraction between the Sun and Proxima Centauri.
hints: Hint 1: Once you have the field strength at the Sun's position, think how field strength is defined in terms of force on a mass placed there.
Hint 2: Multiply the mass of the Sun by the field strength from (b)(ii)1, giving $F$ in $\text{N}$ to 2 s.f.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Force on the Sun**
Field strength is force per unit mass, so force on mass $m$: $$F = m g$$ With Sun mass $m = 2.0 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$ and $g = 1.0 \times 10^{-14} \text{ N kg}^{-1}$: $$F = 2.0 \times 10^{30} \times 1.0 \times 10^{-14} = 2.0 \times 10^{16} \text{ N}$$ This is the attraction between the Sun and Proxima Centauri.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Suggest quantitatively why it may be assumed that the Sun is isolated in space from other stars.

markscheme_points.text: force (of $2 \times 10^{16} \text{N}$) would have little effect on (large) mass of Sun
would cause an acceleration of Sun of $1.0 \times 10^{-14} \text{m s}^{-2}$/very small/negligible acceleration
or many stars all around the Sun
net effect of forces/fields is zero

hints: Hint 1: Use your value of force from (b)(ii) and think about Newton's second law applied to the very large mass of the Sun.
Hint 2: Calculate or estimate the resulting acceleration of the Sun and decide if such a tiny rate of change of velocity matters in practice.
parts.proper_answer: The $2.0 \times 10^{16} \text{ N}$ force on the large mass of the Sun produces an acceleration of only $1.0 \times 10^{-14} \text{ m s}^{-2}$, which is negligible, so the Sun may be assumed isolated.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Huge force but huger mass**
$2.0 \times 10^{16} \text{ N}$ sounds enormous in everyday terms, but you must compare it with the inertia of the Sun, $2.0 \times 10^{30} \text{ kg}$. From $a = F/m$: $$a = \frac{2.0 \times 10^{16}}{2.0 \times 10^{30}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-14} \text{ m s}^{-2}$$

Step 2: **Why isolated is a good model**
An acceleration of $10^{-14} \text{ m s}^{-2}$ will change the Sun's velocity by a negligible amount even over years. In addition, pulls from many distant stars in different directions largely cancel. So for most calculations the Sun can be treated as isolated in space.
